title: The Long Move
setting: a 24-hour launderette changing its payment system

post.author: u/spin_cycle_tuuli
post.title: I'm the night attendant at a 24-hour launderette. At 23:14 a customer showed me two charges for one wash. The second came from a payment system that isn't live on her machine.

blocks.text: I'm Tuuli, night attendant at the Tumblewell Launderette: 24 washing machines, open all hours. I work 22:00 to 06:00. By day nobody works here; customers pay by card at each machine. Mr Adebayo, whose launderette it is, is away until Monday.

A payment system is the program that takes a card payment and starts a machine. Ours is old, so Mr Adebayo is moving to a new one, Tapwren, in steps: move one group of machines, watch it, move the next, and switch the old one off when none is left. Machines 1 to 3 moved first; 4 to 6 move on Monday, then 7 to 24. It's called the strangler fig, after a vine that grows around a tree until the tree can go.

A setting in Tapwren, the router, says which system owns each group. Only the owner should take money for that group's washes. Moving a group back to the old system takes a minute from his phone: his way back.

Machines 4 to 24 run in shadow mode, a kind of rehearsal. In steps: the machine sends the payment to the old system, which charges the card, taking the money, and starts the wash. A copy goes to Tapwren, which works out what it would charge. The two answers are compared. Only the old system is meant to act.

To charge a card, a system needs keys: secret codes from the card company. Test keys make pretend charges; live keys take real money. Tapwren reads its keys from one settings file. Since Saturday 29 August it had said: machines 1 to 3, live; every other machine, test.

At 06:00 today, Saturday 10 October, Mr Adebayo got 4 to 6 ready for Monday. From home he opened the settings file, changed the line for every other machine from test to live, and saved it. Tapwren used it from the next payment. He posted in our staff chat: "Live keys on, 4 to 6 ready."

At 23:14, just over an hour into my shift, Teodozja brought me her phone from machine 5. Her banking app had pinged twice for one wash: £4.50 to TUMBLEWELL LAUNDERETTE at 22:59, and £4.50 to TAPWREN*TUMBLEWELL at 23:14. The notice over machines 1 to 3 says their charges show as TAPWREN*TUMBLEWELL. Machine 5 isn't one of them.
Tapwren handles shadow copies in a queue, a waiting line, that runs 15 minutes behind the machines, so comparing never slows a wash. Most customers pay, load up and leave.

I taped OUT OF ORDER on 4 to 24 and rang Mr Adebayo: voicemail. On the shop tablet I opened Tapwren's log, its running list of what it did. Each line: the time, the machine, the old and new charge, whether they matched, and what Tapwren did.

06:19:00  machine 4  old £4.50  new £4.50  match     sent, live keys
06:29:00  machine 6  old £3.50  new £4.50  MISMATCH  sent, live keys
...
23:14:00  machine 5  old £4.50  new £4.50  match     sent, live keys
23:14:00  today: 212 shadow charges sent, £954.00
Tapwren isn't live on machines 4 to 24. It charged 212 of my customers anyway.

Shadow copies on machines 4 to 24 are pretend until 06:00 and send real charges from 06:00 to 23:14. Machines 1 to 3 run on Tapwren all day. Nobody is on site until the night attendant's shift starts at 22:00. Markers: the live keys at 06:00, the first second charge at 06:19, the shift at 22:00, Teodozja's second charge at 23:14.

blocks.caption: Redrawn from Tapwren's log and our staff chat, Saturday 10 October 2026. Green is test keys and pretend shadow charges; red is live keys and real ones. Between 06:00 and 23:14, 21 machines (4 to 24) ran 212 washes, 10 each and 11 on machines 4 and 5, about 45 minutes a wash. Each shadow copy reached Tapwren 15 minutes after the wash was paid and charged the card again: 212 x £4.50 = £954.

blocks.text: 212 customers since 06:00, one wash each, charged twice: £954 in second charges. Mr Adebayo is back on Monday morning. What should he change before Monday's move?

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: Look at the second charge, not the first. Which system sent it, with which keys, and what told that system it could send anything at all? Then read the settings file the way Tapwren does: which line does machine 5 fall under? Something a program does to the world outside itself, like taking money, is called a side effect.

replies.author: u/spin_cycle_tuuli
replies.text: Tapwren sent it, with live keys. Its shadow copy runs the same payment step as machines 1 to 3, and nothing told it not to. Machine 5 falls under "every other machine". And the MISMATCH lines are all machine 6, our small one: £3.50 on the old system, £4.50 on Tapwren's price list. Ten today. Nobody had opened the log in six weeks.

comments.author: u/real_as_live_aukusti
comments.text: Shadow traffic, real customers' requests copied to a new system, is only worth anything if it's as real as possible. Test keys say yes to every card, so six weeks on test keys proved nothing about the card company. It has to hit the real thing. Keep the live keys and refund the doubles, sending the money back, every morning. Everyone has it back by breakfast.

replies.author: u/spin_cycle_tuuli
replies.text: Mr Adebayo might like that. Nothing to undo before Monday.

comments.author: u/one_night_kerttu
comments.text: Two systems side by side is the bug. Every day both run, one can do something the other doesn't know about. Move all 24 machines to Tapwren tonight, switch the old system off, and only one system ever charges a card.

reply.prompt: Mr Adebayo is back on Monday morning, and 4 to 6 are due to move that day. What should he change first? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: In shadow mode, let the new system only work out its charge and log it, never send it.
options.part2: On Monday 12 October Mr Adebayo changed three things before the move. Tapwren's shadow copies now work out their charge, compare it and log it, and never send it to the card company. The router decides which system owns each group, and only the owner may take money. And the settings file has one line per group, never one for every other machine: live keys for 1 to 3, and for 4 to 6 only from their move. In the sim, replaying Saturday with shadow copies that only log and keys per group: 0 double charges, and 10 mismatches logged, all machine 6, old £3.50 and Tapwren £4.50. He read the log for the first time, fixed machine 6's price in Tapwren, refunded the 212, and moved 4 to 6 at 10:00. The comparisons on 7 to 24 stayed clean for two weeks, and they moved on Monday 26 October.
options.senior: A shadow copy is there to answer one question: would the new system have done the same? It needs real input for that, and no real effect at all. So the shadow path works out its answer, compares and logs, and the step that talks to the card company is switched off in the code, not just pointed at test keys. A router names one owner per group, and only the owner acts. Keys follow the router, one line per group, so a change meant for 4 to 6 can't reach 7 to 24. And someone reads the comparison log before each move: that is what it is for.

options.text: Refund every double charge each morning, so no customer is out of pocket for long.
options.part2: Mr Adebayo kept the live keys and set Tapwren to refund every double charge at 07:00 each morning. In the sim, replaying Saturday with morning refunds: still 212 double charges, £954.00 refunded at 07:00 on Sunday, and 212 customers who had each seen two charges first. On Monday 4 to 6 moved to Tapwren, but 7 to 24 kept their shadow copies and kept charging twice: on a day like Saturday, 180 doubles. By the weekend two regulars had moved to the coin launderette on the high street, and the card company had written to ask why so many of his payments came back.
options.senior: A refund is a second payment, not an undo: the customer still saw two charges, and some will have gone overdrawn or cancelled the card before 07:00. It treats the symptom every day and leaves the cause, a shadow copy with a side effect, in place. The card company also notices a shop that refunds a large share of its charges. Fix the shadow path so the doubles never happen; refund the ones that did, once.

options.text: Skip the shadow copies and move one group of machines at a time, with a quick way back.
options.part2: Mr Adebayo turned the shadow copies off and moved one group at a time, with the router as his way back. In the sim, replaying Saturday with 4 to 6 on Tapwren, no shadow copies and live keys only for Tapwren's groups: 0 double charges and nothing logged. But machine 6's 10 washes are charged £4.50 instead of £3.50, and nothing compares them to notice. 4 to 6 moved on Monday. On Thursday night a regular showed me her receipts from machine 6: £1 more each time. He fixed the price, refunded the difference and flipped nothing back, because nothing else had gone wrong. This time.
options.senior: Moving a small group at a time with a fast way back is a real migration method, and it does stop the double charges. The price is that real money flows through new code before anything has shown it agrees with the old: the way back only helps once someone notices, and machine 6's wrong price is quiet. For a payment system, keep the comparison and remove the side effect instead; skip shadowing only where the old and new answers are cheap to check by hand.

options.text: Move all 24 machines to the new system tonight, so only one system ever charges a card.
options.part2: On Sunday night Mr Adebayo moved all 24 machines to Tapwren from his phone and switched the old system off. In the sim, replaying Saturday with all 24 at once: 0 double charges, 0 comparisons, and 212 washes on 4 to 24 charged by new code nothing had checked, machine 6's 10 at £4.50 instead of £3.50. One evening that week Tapwren stopped taking cards for most of an hour. With the old system off, there was no group to flip back, and every machine in the shop stood still.
options.senior: One system does end the double charges, but a big bang moves every machine onto unproven code at once and throws away both the comparison and the way back. Every bug the shadow copies would have shown arrives at full size, on all 24 machines, with nothing to fall back to. The double charge came from a side effect in the shadow path, not from having two systems; fix that, and the gradual move keeps its safety.

sim.title: Replay Saturday at the Tumblewell
sim.lede: You're Mr Adebayo on Monday, replaying Saturday 10 October 2026 from 06:00, as the live keys go on, to 23:14. As given data: 24 machines in three groups: 1 to 3 owned by Tapwren, 4 to 6 next, 7 to 24 last. The old system charges £4.50 a wash, £3.50 on machine 6; Tapwren's price list says £4.50 for every machine. Machines 4 and 5 run 11 washes and every other machine 10: 212 on 4 to 24, from 06:04 to Teodozja's at 22:59, and 30 on 1 to 3. Tapwren handles each shadow copy 15 minutes after the wash is paid. Set the keys, whether a shadow copy may send its charge (a side effect), which system the router gives 4 to 6 and 7 to 24, the move plan and morning refunds, then step 15 minutes at a time or play to 23:14.
sim.tryThis: Try this: play it as built: 212 double charges, £954.00, the last at 23:14 on machine 5, and 10 mismatches logged for machine 6. Set the keys to test for every machine but 1 to 3, the six weeks before: 0 doubles. Let a shadow copy only work out and log its charge, with live keys per group: 0 doubles, 10 mismatches logged. Turn on morning refunds: £954.00 back on Sunday, 212 customers who saw two charges. Groups without shadow copies, 4 to 6 on Tapwren: 0 doubles, nothing logged, machine 6 charged £4.50 ten times. All 24 at once: 212 washes on new code, none compared. Router 4 to 6 to Tapwren alone: still 180 doubles on 7 to 24.

explain.oneLine: Nothing went wrong in the old system. Tapwren, running in shadow beside it, did more than work out a charge: it sent one, and only test keys had kept that harmless for six weeks. At 06:00 one line in a shared settings file made the keys live for every machine, and 212 shadow copies took real money.

steps.title: The long move: a strangler fig, one group at a time.
steps.text: A strangler fig replaces an old system piece by piece instead of all at once. First, a router sends one group's payments to the new system, which becomes that group's owner; 1 to 3 went first. What can go wrong: the router and everything else must agree on who owns what. Second, watch that group's real charges and complaints for a while. Third, move the next group, 4 to 6 on Monday, then 7 to 24, with the router as the way back if a group misbehaves. Fourth, when no group is left on the old system, switch it off. The Migration That Ate Tuesday changed one column inside one database by expand and contract; this move is between two whole systems, and the rehearsal for each group runs in the other system, out of sight.

steps.title: The shadow copy that acted.
steps.text: Shadow traffic, in steps: first, copy each real request to the new system. Second, the new system works out its answer. Third, compare it with the old system's answer. Fourth, log any mismatch. Fifth, use only the old answer and never let the new one act. Tapwren did steps one to four, then ran its normal payment step and sent the charge, a side effect. Test keys made it pretend, so for six weeks nothing showed. The settings switch at 06:00 went: open the file, change the line for every other machine from test to live, save; Tapwren read it at the next payment. That one line covered 21 machines, 4 to 24, not just 4 to 6. They ran 212 washes by 23:14, each charged again 15 minutes later, while nobody was on site and most customers had gone.

steps.title: Dual writes and backfills: moving what the old system remembers.
steps.text: Charges are only half a payment system; it also keeps records, such as the history of every wash and each customer's stamp card (one stamp a wash, the tenth free). A dual write keeps both stores current while both are live: first, every new record is written to the old store; second, the same record is written to the new store; third, the two are compared now and then. What can go wrong: one write succeeds and the other fails, so they drift apart. A backfill fills in the past: first, start the dual writes; second, copy the old records across in batches, a slice at a time; third, compare the stores; fourth, move reads, then writes, to the new store; last, stop writing to the old. What can go wrong: a backfill started before the dual writes misses anything written while it runs.

steps.title: The fix: one owner per machine, no side effects in shadow, keys per group.
steps.text: First, the shadow path in Tapwren works out its charge, compares it with the old system's and logs the result, and the step that calls the card company is switched off in the code for shadow copies, whatever the keys say. Second, the router decides which system owns each group, and only the owner may take money. Third, the settings file gets one line per group and none for every other machine, and a group's live keys go on at its move, not before. Rule 3, from The Ticket Number, in one line: "If the register asks you to charge a customer again, check the ticket number first." A ticket number per wash, the number the shop gives each sale, kept in the launderette's own record and checked before any charge is sent, would have shown Tapwren's second charge as a repeat. Then read the log: machine 6's mismatch had been in it every day for six weeks.

steps.title: Why the other fixes fail, and the walk into the other building.
steps.text: Refunds each morning leave 212 customers who saw two charges, and the cause in place. Skipping the shadow copies stops the doubles, but machine 6's wrong price reaches customers with nothing compared to catch it. Moving all 24 at once removes the comparison and the way back together. Running both systems on one bigger server, a computer that runs programs for others, changes where they run, not what they do: the shadow copy still sends its charge. On Monday morning, after her shift, Tuuli stayed on, and she and Mr Adebayo opened Tapwren's settings file together on the shop tablet. The night had started in that other building, one line long: every other machine, live.

diagram.aria: The fix, replayed for Teodozja's wash. At 22:59 machine 5 sends the payment to the router. The router's owner for 4 to 24 is the old system, so the payment goes there, and the old system has the card company charge £4.50. The router also sends a shadow copy to Tapwren. Tapwren works out £4.50 and does not call the card company. The old system's answer, £4.50, reaches Tapwren, which logs a match. Outcome: one charge for one wash.

explain.caption: The fix, replayed for Teodozja's 22:59 wash. The router names the old system as owner of machines 4 to 24, so only the old system asks the card company for money. Tapwren gets a shadow copy, works out the same £4.50, compares it with the old answer and logs a match, and its sending step is switched off for shadow copies.

fix.title: The fix: shadow copies only work out, compare and log; one owner per group; live keys per group
fix.text: Switch off, in Tapwren's code, the step that sends a shadow copy's charge to the card company, so a shadow copy can only work out its answer, compare it with the old system's and log it. Let the router name one owner per group of machines, and let only the owner take money. Give the settings file one line per group, never a line for every other machine, and turn a group's live keys on at its move. Keep the launderette's own ticket number per wash and check it before any charge goes out. Read the comparison log before each move, and move a group only when its log is clean: machine 6's price first.

limits: With its sending step switched off in shadow, Tapwren's real sending is never rehearsed: the first real charge it sends for a group comes on the morning that group moves. Watch the first hour of each move and keep the way back ready.
A comparison only finds what it compares, and only helps if someone reads it. Machine 6's mismatch sat in the log every day for six weeks before anyone opened it.
The router and the keys are now two settings that must agree. A group the router gives Tapwren while its keys are still test takes no real money: 32 washes on 4 to 6 in the sim.

explain.seniorTake: A large migration is mostly about knowing, at every moment, which system is allowed to change the world. Grow the new system around the old one group by group, with a router that names one owner for each group and a way back for each step. Use shadow traffic to learn whether the new system agrees, with real input and no real effect: block side effects in the code, not with a test setting that one edit can flip. Keep secrets and settings per group so a change for the next group can't reach the rest. Move data with dual writes first and a backfill second, compare before you switch, and read the comparisons. The danger in a long move is rarely the old building or the new one; it is the shared wiring between them.

realWorld.title: GitHub's Scientist, 2016: run both, keep the old answer
realWorld.text: Jesse Toth's post on Scientist, GitHub's tool for rewriting critical code, says: "When the experiment is called at runtime, both code paths are run (with the order randomized to avoid ordering issues)." Then "the result of the control code is returned from the experiment." The control is the old code; the candidate is the new. "From the caller’s perspective, nothing has changed."

realWorld.title: Scientist: never with side effects
realWorld.text: "The most important caveat is that Scientist is not meant to be used for any code that has side-effects." And: "A candidate code path that writes to the same database as the control, invalidates a cache, or otherwise modifies data that affects the original, production behavior is dangerous and incorrect." A cache is a store of saved answers; production is the live system real customers use. "For this reason, we only use Scientist on read operations." Tapwren's shadow copy sent a charge.

realWorld.title: Scientist: real input, not real effects
realWorld.text: The same post backs half of Aukusti's point: "So, while test coverage of a rewritten system is hugely important, how the system behaves with production data as the input is the only true test of its correctness compared to the legacy system's behavior." The legacy system is the old one. Real input, then, but the caveat above still rules out real effects.

realWorld.title: Stripe, 2017: dual writes
realWorld.text: Jacqueline Xu's "Online migrations at scale" says: "There’s a common 4 step dual writing pattern that people often use to do large online migrations like this." Step one: "Dual writing to the existing and new tables to keep them in sync." A table is one list of records in a database. "All new writes should update both stores." Then "Changing all read paths in our codebase to read from the new table." and "Changing all write paths in our codebase to only write to the new table."

realWorld.title: Stripe: the backfill comes after the dual writes
realWorld.text: Once the dual writes are on, the post says, "newly created objects exist in both tables, while older objects are only found in the old table." Then: "We’ll then backfill missing data to the new store so the two stores hold identical information." The post shows this order without spelling out why; the reason is that everything new is already in both stores before the copying starts.

realWorld.title: Stripe used Scientist on its reads
realWorld.text: "We’ll use GitHub’s Scientist to help us verify our read paths." And on a difference: "If the results don’t match, raise an error alerting our engineers to the inconsistency." Reads only: compare, raise, never act.

realWorld.title: Martin Fowler: the strangler fig
realWorld.text: Fowler named the pattern after figs he saw in Queensland: "These are vines that germinate in a nook of a tree." "It can then become self-sustaining, and its original host tree may die leaving the fig as an echo of its shape." The term, he writes, "is now often used to describe a gradual approach to legacy modernization." Modernization means replacing an old system with newer technology.

realWorld.title: Fowler: against the big rewrite
realWorld.text: Of building a replacement that does exactly what the old system does, all at once: "But we've seen this simple-sounding plan go down in flames most of the time." Instead: "The alternative that my colleagues and I prefer, is to do a gradual process of modernization."

realWorld.title: Fowler: scaffolding you will throw away
realWorld.text: "When doing this, people often balk at the necessity of building transitional architecture to allow the new and legacy system to coexist, code that will go away once the modernization is complete." "While this may appear to be a waste, the reduced risk and earlier value from the gradual approach outweigh its costs." The router and the shadow copies are the Tumblewell's transitional architecture.

asked: How would you move payments to a new system without downtime?
What is shadow traffic, and what must it never do?
Dual writes or a backfill: when do you use each?
interview.answer: I'd move it as a strangler fig, a group at a time. First, put a router in front that names one owner for each group of users or machines; only the owner may charge a card. Second, before a group moves, send it shadow traffic: copy each real request to the new system, let it work out its answer, compare that with the old system's, log every mismatch, and always use the old answer. Shadow traffic must never act: no charges, no emails, no writes to shared data. I'd block that in the code, not rely on test credentials, because one settings change can make them live, and I'd keep credentials per group. Third, read the mismatches, fix them, then move that group, with the router as a quick way back. Fourth, when no group is left, retire the old system. For stored data, dual writes and backfills work together: start dual writes first, so every new record goes to both stores; then backfill the history in batches; compare the two stores; move reads to the new store, then writes; and only then stop writing to the old. A backfill alone misses whatever is written while it runs; dual writes alone never bring the history across. And every payment carries its own ticket number, an idempotency key, so a repeat is caught. I'd tell the story of a launderette whose shadow system shared one settings file with the live one: a switch meant for three machines made it charge 212 customers a second time.

atWork: Look for any new system running beside an old one on copies of real requests: a rewritten payment, booking, email or stock service. A shadow system that shares live settings with the system it shadows is a common pattern; it stays harmless only until someone changes one shared line. For each one, ask four things. What can the shadow path do outside itself: charge a card, send a message, write to a shared database, clear a cache? Is that blocked in the code, or only by a test setting? Where do its keys and passwords come from, and is there one entry per group, or one for everything? And who reads the comparison log, and when? If your secrets live in a store such as AWS Secrets Manager, check which entries the shadow path can read. Standards: if your company is pursuing SOC 2, processing integrity (PI1), which Linford & Co sums up as "System processing is complete, valid, accurate, timely, and authorized to meet the entity's objectives.", expects each wash or order to be charged once, as stated, so write "shadow paths have no side effects" into the design from the first draft. If it is pursuing ISO/IEC 27001:2022, Annex A 8.32 (change management) is the control an auditor would read the 06:00 settings switch against: a change to live keys should be planned, assessed and tested before it reaches every machine, not made from home on a Saturday.

recall.prompt: Your team is replacing the service that sends order emails. To check the new one, every order request is also copied to it, and only the old service's emails are meant to reach customers. On the day the new service is given the company's real email account, ready for next week's switch, customers start getting two confirmation emails for one order, one from each service. What happened, and what would you change?

keyIdeas.idea: The copy had a side effect: the new service really sent, and only a test setting had kept that harmless
A shadow copy should only work out its answer, compare and log it, never act; block sending in the code
A router names one owner per group, only the owner acts, and real credentials are set per group, not in one shared setting

recall.model: The copy of each order had a side effect: the new service really sent its email, and only its test email account had kept that harmless until the real one was switched on for everything. A shadow copy should only work out its answer, compare it with the old service's and log the difference, and never send; block the sending in the code, not with a setting. Then let a router name one owner for each kind of order, so only the owner sends, and give the real account to each group as it moves, not in one shared setting.

recall.prompt: In the sim, with live keys for every machine and everything else as built, which one change alone stops the double charges and still logs machine 6's mismatches?
options: Refund every double charge at 07:00 the next morning
Let a shadow copy only work out its charge and log it
Move groups without shadow copies, 4 to 6 on Tapwren
Put all 24 machines on Tapwren at once
recall.why: A shadow copy that only works out and logs gives 0 double charges, and machine 6's 10 mismatches still reach the log. Refunds leave 212 doubles that customers saw first. Moving 4 to 6 without shadow copies logs nothing and charges machine 6 the wrong price 10 times; all 24 at once does the same, with 212 washes on new code nothing compared.

recall.prompt: Stripe's post moves records from an old table to a new one while both stay live. In what order does its pattern go?
options: Backfill the old records, then send new ones to old and new, then switch reads
Write to both, backfill, switch reads, then stop writing to the old
Switch reads to the new table, backfill, then send new records to old and new
Write only to the new table, then backfill the old records into it
recall.why: Xu's pattern starts with dual writing, "All new writes should update both stores", then backfills so "the two stores hold identical information", then moves read paths, then write paths, then removes the old data. A backfill run first misses anything written while it runs.

recall.prompt: In an interview you're asked: what is shadow traffic, and what must it never do?

keyIdeas.idea: A copy of real requests goes to the new system, which works out its answer beside the old one
The two answers are compared and mismatches logged; only the old system's answer is used
No side effects: it must never charge, write or send anything for real

recall.model: Shadow traffic sends a copy of real requests to a new system while the old one keeps serving them. The new system works out what it would answer, side by side with the old, and the two answers are compared; every mismatch is logged, and the caller always gets the old system's answer, which GitHub's Scientist calls the control. It must have no side effects: never charge a card, never write to shared data, never send a message, because anything it does for real happens a second time. I'd block that in the code rather than trust a test setting, and keep real credentials per group, set only where the new system is the owner.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 2 months later. All 24 machines charge through Tapwren now, once a wash, and the old payment system is off. The stamp cards came last: one stamp a wash, the tenth wash free. They still lived in the old system's database, where Tapwren added each new stamp. On Tuesday 1 December, from 01:00 to 03:10, Mr Adebayo ran a job that copied every card's stamps into Tapwren's own store, 100 cards at a time, and at 03:10 Tapwren switched to its own store. By Saturday 5 December, 14 customers had shown me cards a stamp short, and every missing stamp was from a wash between 01:00 and 03:10.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Why are 14 stamps missing, and how should the next move of stored records be done?

keyIdeas.idea: The backfill copied each card once; stamps added to the old store after that card's batch never reached the new store
Dual write first: every new stamp goes to both stores before and during the backfill
Compare the two stores and switch reads only when they agree; keep the old store until then

coldCase.model: The job was a backfill with no dual writes. It copied each card once, in batches; any stamp a customer earned after their card's batch had been copied went only into the old database, and at 03:10 Tapwren stopped reading it. Those stamps stayed in the old store, and 14 of them were missed. Next time, start a dual write first: from that moment every new stamp is written to both stores. Then run the backfill, then compare the two stores card by card, and switch Tapwren's reads only when they agree, keeping the old store until then. Then stop writing to the old one, and only after that switch it off. The 14 stamps are still in the old database, so copy them across now.
